newsitem.title: USA: Simpson jury deliberates for second day.
newsitem.headline: Simpson jury deliberates for second day.

text.p: Jurors in O.J. Simpson's civil trial deliberated for a second day on Wednesday to decide if the former American football star was responsible for the murders of his ex-wife and her friend.

The panel's first request to the judge came just before the lunch break when they asked for a small magnifying glass used to examine photographs, as well as a picture of a test tube like the one that contained a sample of Simpson's blood taken by police the day after the murders.

Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki gave them the magnifying device but told them they already had inside the jury room such a test tube as part of the evidence given to them when they began deliberating on Tuesday, a court spokeswoman said.

The written request sparked speculation about where the jury might be headed in its deliberations. The panel of seven women and five men, confined to a cramped, windowless room, remained behind closed doors early on Wednesday afternoon.
Simpson's defence team claims police, seeking to frame the former athlete, smeared some of his blood from the test tube at the murder scene in his Ford Bronco and in his mansion.
The magnifying device could also be used by jurors to examine photographs of Simpson wearing Bruno Magli shoes similar to ones that left bloody prints at the murder scene.

Jurors deliberated for about two hours on Tuesday after receiving instructions from Fujisaki, who told them to ignore the fact that Simpson was cleared of the June 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman by a criminal court jury in October 1995.
The jurors were also directed to disregard the recent ruling of a family court giving Simpson custody of his two children, Sydney and Justin, who had been living with Nicole Brown Simpson's parents.

It took just under four hours for the jury to surpass the time it took Simpson's criminal trial jury to reach a not-guilty verdict. Simpson is battling a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims, who are seeking substantial damages.
As the jury met, there was a brief hearing in the judge's chambers in which he granted a plaintiffs' motion forcing the defence to disclose more of Simpson's financial assets.
The jury of nine whites, one Hispanic, one black and an Asian-black, armed with a stack of notebooks and more than 600 pieces of evidence, have a complicated task in front of them.

First they must decide if Simpson "willfully and wrongfully" caused Goldman's death. If the answer is yes they must then decide if he committed "battery" against Goldman and if that was accompanied by "malice" and "oppression."

But the jurors are not being asked to say whether Simpson caused the death of his ex-wife. Instead they are being asked to find if he battered her in the deadly attack and if oppression and malice were involved.

According to the judge's instructions, oppression involves an attack that was carried out in a "base, vile, contemptible, wretched, loathsome or miserable" manner that "ordinary, decent people" would recoil from.

While Goldman's father, Fred Goldman, is suing Simpson on behalf of the family, Nicole Brown Simpson's father, Lou Brown, is suing as executor of his daughter's estate, the beneficiaries of which are Simpson's two young children.
Under California law, an estate cannot sue for wrongful death. It can, however, sue for punitive damages.

Unlike a criminal trial, the jury's decision does not have to be unanimous and it may decide the case by a 9-3 majority. Also it only has to find on the basis of a "preponderance of evidence" rather than the "beyond a reasonable doubt" standard applied to criminal cases.
